title: Earth, cry, and the witness in heaven
english: He appeals to the mountains, suggesting that they possess knowledge of things existing before the creation of the world [[Job 27:6 >> Bible:Job 27:6]]. In chapters 1, 17, and 18, he cries out, 'Earth, do not cover my eyes from my physical sight, nor let there be a place for my cry to echo; behold, my witness is in the heavens, and my supporter is in the highest heights.' As he wanders toward the earth, he reasons and calls out for sympathy, uttering words that are profoundly well-spoken. He says, 'O earth, do not remain silent regarding my plight, nor secretly conceal the blood unjustly shed from my flesh through my wounds; do not stand in a place and hide, nor let the memory of my lamentations fall into oblivion; for many have indeed been built up through my trials.' He continues, 'Let not the earth hide my blood, but let it summon God to vengeance, with the wounds of my body serving as witnesses. Let not the air restrain my cry, but let the sound of my voice reach the heavens, so that God, the avenger of these occurring evils, may stand forth. By defending the guilty, you will demonstrate to all the blamelessness of my conduct.' He adds, 'Behold, my witness in the heavens is purer than the human conscience' [[Job 19:3 >> Bible:Job 19:3]].

He instructs, 'Only know that the Lord has brought this upon me.' He speaks this to strike fear into them, saying, 'Do not trample upon me while I suffer, lest you yourselves fall into the same condition, sharing the same human nature' [[Job 4:5, 5:7 >> Bible:Job 4:5, 5:7]]. 'Truly, I have been led astray; yet the deceiver mocks me, speaking words that should never have been uttered, and he misrepresents my words and speaks them out of season. Let you magnify yourselves at my expense and reproach me. Let it be assumed, as a hypothesis, that I was deceived. But the deceiver mocks me; the deceiver is the devil. What harm comes to you from this? Why is it necessary to judge me as impious and to trample upon one in pain? It is necessary to show compassion to one speaking through agony.' He asks, 'If even such things were done that were not necessary, was it then necessary for you to reproach me so?' He says, 'Having long ago devoted myself to piety, it is necessary for me now to have a reputation based on my works. I have not done this, yet I am judged as a deceiver.' This applies here as well [[Job 7:6 >> Bible:Job 7:6]].

He declares, 'Know then that the Lord is the one who has troubled me; He has raised His weapon against me. Behold, I will laugh at your reproaches, but I will not speak. I have cried out, yet no judgment comes. Reason with yourselves; I am not made without purpose, though I feel as if I am encircled by a terrible wall. I speak the truth regarding my circumstances, yet you refuse to accept my words.' He explains that his refusal to speak is not because he has nothing to say, but rather because he feels that since you oppose me, it is better to remain silent. 'Even if I cry out to God to make my situation clear to everyone, I find no favor. No one listens, no one judges, I see no one, and I have nowhere to flee. Should these things not be pitied?' He suggests that by unrighteously mocking him, they allow God to stand as judge to execute a sentence of irrational destruction upon them. 'I do not flee,' he says, 'for God does not abandon such things.' He implies that what appears to you as an unlearned opinion regarding the knowledge of good and the things to come will eventually be proven true. He asks, 'What do you say to the fact that I suffer these things while in wickedness? You yourselves ought to fear the same.' He urges, 'Hurry, even while these things are testifying through words; grasp hold of the words so that you might not be judged as unrighteous even by the truth itself.'

The Hebrew text contains a sin of the word [[Job 21:1 >> Bible:Job 21:1]]. Having killed his lesser sons, and with his hands having burned the soles, he says those before him—those more inferior—will cast down the children of the lawless [[Job 14:14 >> Bible:Job 14:14]]. Wealth gathered unjustly will be scrutinized, and an angel will drag the man from his house. The impious man does everything to seize the possessions of others, and one looks at the purpose of these events through him; yet when he seems to be master of all, he will see himself being carried away to others [[Job 16:14 >> Bible:Job 16:14]]. Like an unplowed, uncontrollable plow, the words and doctrines of the impious are crooked and deceptive, for there is nothing sweet in things that happen against God [[Job 22:22 >> Bible:Job 22:22]]. But when he seems to be full, he will be crushed, and necessity will press upon him. He says that because of the cause, acquired things are being stripped away and will not be passed to his ancestors [[Job 23:12 >> Bible:Job 23:12]]. A spirit of wrath will be sent upon him to pour out his soles [[Job 23:16 >> Bible:Job 23:16]]. Instead, he will undergo terrible things from God and heaven. He said this because Job, having claimed he was struck by God, also remembered how he was wronged by men; thus, he prepares, knowing that all things were brought upon him through sin [[Job 24:24 >> Bible:Job 24:24]]. And stars in the diets...

title: The Nature of Wickedness and the Office of the Bishop
english: They wander about in ignorance, for the light has emanated from within themselves, even as He declared: [[quote >> John 8:12 >> I am the light of the world]]. An unconsuming fire shall fall upon him. Regarding the hidden meaning, this unconsuming fire refers either to the conscience or to the judgments that await the righteous in the future. He says that the man shall be consumed by fire so that it may be said he is not even worthy of a burial.

This is the portion assigned to the impious man by the Lord, and it is a possession held by those under the bishop. Through this, divine justice is set in motion against him, whether he is one who, though circumcised, acted impiously toward God through Christ, or whether he is a paradoxical person; regardless, the declared portion belongs to the impious. Consider who the bishop mentioned here was. It is said that God is the Bishop, and the bishops of God strive to imitate His likeness in every way, being good and noble. Just as one who imitates a royal icon is honored for the excellence of his imitation and for the beauty he adds to it, so too is the blessed bishop who has perceived the true Bishop and follows Him with zeal. Such a man becomes like God among men; or, alternatively, he is one who possesses a bishop who truly makes him a bishop in Christ Jesus, to whom belong the glory and the dominion forever and ever. Amen.

Their children also play, taking up the psaltery and the lyre, finding joy in the sound of psalmody. Indeed, even their foolish children engage in such play, for they sing the psalms of Valentinus and the hymns of Basileidus, finding delight in the melody of their songs.

Is not the Lord the one who imparts understanding and knowledge? Let us observe what Eliphaz says to the righteous man. After Job has spoken, Eliphaz rushes to join the argument, saying: I also know that God alone is wise, and that through certain words one impious man is corrected while another is punished. I also know that God is the giver of good things, as you have said, whereas evil brings about punishment. This doctrine is healthy. Knowledge is the comprehension of those who possess such a theory, while understanding is the power of distinction.

Is it not possible that your wickedness is great and your sins are beyond counting? It is therefore expected that I should say you have not become unrighteous by mere chance because you suffer such things as no other wicked man does; rather, you have fallen into these circumstances because you possess a greater wickedness than others. Wickedness is an evil disposition of the soul, such as grief, anger, or disordered desire, whereas sin is the actual exercise of that disposition. Therefore, he first mentioned wickedness and then sin—the former being a great state and the latter being innumerable acts. I see many sinners, yet none have fallen into such profound depths as you have. It is probable that because of your countless sins and your multitude of faults, these things have befallen you. You were defrauding your brothers through usury, and you were stripping the naked of their clothing. Let us take heed, O engravers, that we never defraud others through lending. These words are useful, for they allow us to speak truthfully about sins as they occur among men according to reason. Eliphaz assumes this regarding Job because he knew Job was wealthy and suspected he might have acquired his riches through improper means; thus he says: You were defrauding by lending, meaning you left nothing unpaid. If I lend money but, distrusting the borrower, I take a pledge of great value as security, that is not true lending. But if I demand and seize a pledge by lending because I slander him, claiming he cannot pay his debts, then I am lending. He adds another suspected sin: it is possible to take garments not from the naked, but from the rich who have many clothes lying around. Yet, if a man has only a single tunic and I use that as a pretext to demand my property, I strip him; having no pity for the naked man, I have deprived him of his clothing. Many such things occur among us when we lend or visit debtors. Often the debtor falls into such excess that he cannot pay, and we, becoming hardened and pitiless, fail to see that a woman must feed children on the few coins provided, and we demand payment bitterly even when we ourselves live in abundance. Such bitter demands occur...

title: Accountability for Inaction
english: Someone possesses a piece of bread; if they lack a whole loaf, we take it from them, declaring, 'But you owe.' Thus, he accuses Job, asserting that he stripped the naked of their garments. Not only did you fail to quench the thirst of the parched, but you denied the hungry their sustenance. You favored certain faces, displacing the poor from their dwellings. Widows you sent away empty-handed, and orphans you left in misery. To wrong another is one transgression, but to withhold kindness is equally culpable. The text emphasizes that our duty extends to aiding the desperate, as even the simple act of offering water to the thirsty incurs divine accountability. Though a cup of cold water earns a reward, Job's stubbornness is condemned for withholding even basic charity from the thirsty. The hungry you deprived of bread—what need is there to elaborate? When you deny the beggar even a morsel, you commit a grave sin. Bread, as defined here, refers to a fragment of the loaf, as seen in the passage: 'Dip your bread in the vinegar.'

You admired certain faces, rendering judgments not with fairness or impartiality, but with human bias, becoming a mere spectator of appearances. You elevated the powerful while humiliating the meek, forcing the humble and honoring the mighty. You displaced the poor, as some manuscripts suggest 'you laid them to rest' instead of 'lodged them,' implying the theft of their meager beds. Widows you expelled without mercy, and orphans you left destitute. To harm the defenseless is the epitome of wickedness. No one should inflict harm, especially not the orphans, for God commands protection for the helpless. The poor, widows, and orphans require greater compassion than others. The counsel of the wicked lies far from God, and the righteous mock their schemes. What the wicked plan is distant from divine truth. The one who casts a curse from his mouth urges others to internalize his words. They sought redemption in me—what does this mean? In another version, it reads 'confession' instead of 'redemption.' From Akylas, 'Law' is cited. One interpretation urges confession of sins, while another commands receiving God's law and embracing His words. If just and worthy, one is proclaimed by God, receiving divine utterances from the heart, as Jeremiah was told: 'Behold, I have placed my words in your mouth.' Redemption through confession exhorts the righteous to repent. Alternatively, it may mean adopting divine laws or atoning for sins while preserving God's teachings. The dual meaning of redemption stems from these interpretations.
